body.statement: For two size-three clusters, \(K=2\), \(r_{3,1}=1\), \(r_{3,2}=2\), and coefficient order \((c_{1,1},c_{0,1},c_{1,2},c_{0,2})=(3,-1,-1,-1)\), a rational 78-decision procedure and a 17-orbit prior certify \(1.3649753<R^\star\le1.364981422\) with primal-dual gap below \(10^{-5}\), while a 15-orbit prior certifies \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}>1.3659\). Thus \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}-R^\star>0.000918578\). For every rational \(t\) with \(|t|\le10^{-5}\), replacing \(c\) by \((3+t,-1-t,-1,-1)\) preserves \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}-R^\star>7\times10^{-4}\).
body.justification: The rational separation proves that cross-cluster correlation can lower unrestricted minimax risk, not merely the variance of a selected linear estimator.
body.gap: Hull2026's independent-design theorem relies on a no-interference tensorization, and CaiPougetAbadieAiroldi2022 optimizes a conventional estimator; the certified saturation instance permits every measurable estimator on both sides.
body.consumer: The result supplies a concrete reason for BairdBohrenMcIntoshOzler2018-style trials to consider correlated saturation labels when robust finite-population MSE is the design criterion.
body.proof_tex:
All quantities in this proof are rational and are evaluated using the orbit kernel already proved in \(\texttt{thm:endpoint-orbit-equivalence}\).  We display enough data to reproduce the certificate.

Encode a unit's four binary responses in the order \((1,1),(0,1),(1,2),(0,2)\) as the four low-to-high bits of an integer in \(\{0,\ldots,15\}\).  A size-three cluster type is a nondecreasing triple of these integers.  There are
\[
 T=\binom{16+3-1}{3}=816
\]
cluster types and \(\binom{816+1}{2}=333336\) two-cluster response orbits.  At label one, index a local outcome by \(k=3u+v\); at label two, index it by \(k=2u+v\).  Both indices range from zero to five.  The assignment orbits \(11,12,22\) consequently have \(21,36,21\) observation orbits, for a total of \(78\).

For a cluster type \(t\), let \(C_{a,t,k}\) be the number, among the three feasible exact-count subsets at label \(a\), that produce local index \(k\).  Thus \(P_{t,a}(k)=C_{a,t,k}/3\).  For an unordered pair \(\{t,t'\}\), define the integer likelihood row \(M_{tt',j}\), \(0\le j<78\), by
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 M_{tt',\{k,l\}_{11}}=2\{C_{1,t,k}C_{1,t',l}+\mathbf1_{k<l}C_{1,t,l}C_{1,t',k}\},& k\le l,\\
 M_{tt',(k,l)_{12}}=C_{1,t,k}C_{2,t',l}+C_{1,t',k}C_{2,t,l},&0\le k,l<6,\\
 M_{tt',\{k,l\}_{22}}=2\{C_{2,t,k}C_{2,t',l}+\mathbf1_{k<l}C_{2,t,l}C_{2,t',k}\},& k\le l.
\end{array}                                                               \tag{35}
\]
For each assignment block, the entries in (35) sum to \(18\), and \(M_{tt',j}/18\) is exactly the corresponding orbit likelihood.  Formula (35) is the specialization of the coefficient identity (12), including the two equally likely cluster-label orientations in orbit \(12\).

Use design masses
\[
 (q_{11},q_{12},q_{22})={1\over10^8}(50372138,42844038,6783824),             \tag{36}
\]
and, in the order upper-triangular \(11\), rectangular \(12\), upper-triangular \(22\), use endpoint decisions \(d_j=e_j/10^5\), where
\[
\begin{split}
(e_j)_{j=0}^{77}={}&(-78795,-99673,-125925,42873,13619,-28110,-131707,-161503,
21409,0,-22496,-189980,0,-21409,-43058,189980,161503,123041,131707,100384,81531,\\
&47551,0,-31307,-33852,-14286,-109350,21499,-22463,-30459,-80795,-69654,-145451,5723,
-93539,-52330,-155278,-89207,-178491,178491,71330,171200,14818,67123,-5722,\\
&145451,90301,68712,21192,47169,-21499,134172,-16612,102456,-11008,6753,-51501,
165520,114346,101636,42573,20700,0,65736,36413,50311,0,-93454,-33333,-33333,\\
&33333,-62461,1415,-49421,-150652,0,9511,-165520).
\end{split}                                                               \tag{37}
\]
Every entry in (37) lies in \([-3\cdot10^5,3\cdot10^5]\), so the rule is clipped.  If \(T(t)=\sum_{i,z,a}c_{z,a}Y_i(z,a)\), then the target for \(\{t,t'\}\) is \((T(t)+T(t'))/6\), and \(-18\le T(t)+T(t')\le18\).

For an integer target numerator \(h\in[-18,18]\) and cell \(j\), with \(g(j)\in\{11,12,22\}\), put
\[
 A_{h,j}=\left\lceil
 {q_{g(j)}(6e_j-10^5h)^2\,10^9\over(6\cdot10^5)^2}
 \right\rceil.                                                            \tag{38}
\]
Here the \(q\)'s in (38) are the rational probabilities in (36).  Summing (38) with the exact subset and orientation multiplicities in (35), over each of the \(333336\) response orbits, gives
\[
 \max_{t\le t'}{1\over18\cdot10^9}
 \sum_{j=0}^{77}M_{tt',j}A_{T(t)+T(t'),j}
 ={682490711\over500000000}.                                               \tag{39}
\]
Because each ceiling in (38) is outward, (39) proves the rigorous upper bound
\[
 R^\star\le {682490711\over500000000}=1.364981422.                          \tag{40}
\]
Equation (39) is an exhaustive integer check: the cluster types are the lexicographic triples \(0\le j_1\le j_2\le j_3\le15\), the response pairs are their upper triangle, and (35), (38) use only integer addition, multiplication, division with remainder, and a maximum.

For the unrestricted lower certificate, put prior mass equal to the displayed numerator divided by \(9999999\) on each response orbit in the following table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|r}
t&t'&\text{numerator}\\\hline
(0,0,3)&(13,13,13)&93579\\
(0,1,3)&(0,1,3)&32185\\
(0,1,3)&(0,3,3)&4627\\
(0,1,3)&(1,1,1)&1175451\\
(0,3,3)&(0,3,3)&1277354\\
(0,3,3)&(13,13,13)&937059\\
(1,1,1)&(1,1,1)&704115\\
(2,2,2)&(2,2,2)&501848\\
(2,2,2)&(12,12,15)&937061\\
(2,2,2)&(12,15,15)&93580\\
(2,2,2)&(13,13,13)&547561\\
(12,12,15)&(12,12,15)&1277355\\
(12,12,15)&(12,14,15)&4624\\
(12,14,15)&(12,14,15)&32186\\
(12,14,15)&(14,14,14)&1175451\\
(13,13,13)&(13,13,13)&501848\\
(14,14,14)&(14,14,14)&704115
\end{array}                                                               \tag{41}
\]
The numerators in (41) sum to \(9999999\).  Substitution of (35) and the targets into the posterior-variance formula (18) gives, for \(11,12,22\), respectively,
\[
\begin{split}
B_{11}&={15375502988468197921840146383881271727233984862425002228885431140677343747
\over11264307876254729959135311641689644340133922991873868807613042371771565600},\\
B_{12}&={448449106336744246211520343854236088916292823478774594883
\over328540052093168094561750909236330942644710693505276887705},\\
B_{22}&={875407001549306027053357121
\over641335093640491500999272160}.
\end{split}                                                               \tag{42}
\]
Direct cross multiplication in (42) gives \(B_{11}>13649753/10^7\), \(B_{12}>13649753/10^7\), and \(B_{22}>13649753/10^7\).  The dual identity (19) therefore proves
\[
 R^\star>{13649753\over10^7}=1.3649753.                                    \tag{43}
\]
Equations (40) and (43) also give a primal--dual gap smaller than \(10^{-5}\).

For the independent lower certificate, put mass equal to the displayed numerator divided by \(10000001\) on the following fifteen response orbits:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|r}
t&t'&\text{numerator}\\\hline
(0,1,3)&(0,1,3)&22021\\
(0,1,3)&(1,1,1)&1206305\\
(0,2,3)&(13,13,13)&96393\\
(0,3,3)&(0,3,3)&1290697\\
(0,3,3)&(13,13,13)&922076\\
(1,1,1)&(1,1,1)&693092\\
(2,2,2)&(2,2,2)&570855\\
(2,2,2)&(12,12,15)&922076\\
(2,2,2)&(12,13,15)&96391\\
(2,2,2)&(13,13,13)&397129\\
(12,12,15)&(12,12,15)&1290696\\
(12,14,15)&(12,14,15)&22012\\
(12,14,15)&(14,14,14)&1206312\\
(13,13,13)&(13,13,13)&570855\\
(14,14,14)&(14,14,14)&693091
\end{array}                                                               \tag{44}
\]
The numerators in (44) sum to \(10000001\).  Its three conditional Bayes risks from (18) are
\[
\begin{split}
b_0&={510475303939035976629005312819976017636302495199788360789626523726439
\over369944115755171414919449929497305596423215368453011019149630652456016},\\
b_1&={1481174023898820321516133538462560606861100123434633
\over1112403418358068410799836111119084211132456048612006},\\
b_2&={151645559092055579448236753
\over104500605048826858776739890}.
\end{split}                                                               \tag{45}
\]
If \(p\) is the common probability of label one, every estimator has Bayes risk at least
\[
 q(p)=b_0p^2+2b_1p(1-p)+b_2(1-p)^2.                                       \tag{46}
\]
Exact cross multiplication in (45) shows \(A=b_0-2b_1+b_2>0\) and \(0<(b_2-b_1)/A<1\).  Thus completing the square in (46) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \min_{0\le p\le1}q(p)
 &=b_2-{(b_2-b_1)^2\over A}\\
 &={15905203453139106542517135433476445901965288230411009200606834963558543472086380998618525138518327606158980351835088763299728100108165337352676095029503340442637423716141827041
\over11644070726222582883296696074226046164046332571505009828610177241754496145584750907986901385009654041984574087952923135008216678502549249251959833183001560101499077844672521234}\\
 &>{13659\over10000}.
\end{aligned}                                                               \tag{47}
\]
The Bayes lower bound in (47) holds for every nonlinear estimator and every \(p\), including \(p=0,1\).  Hence \(R_{\mathrm{ind}}>1.3659\).  Combining this with (40) proves
\[
 R_{\mathrm{ind}}-R^\star>1.3659-1.364981422=0.000918578.                  \tag{48}
\]

Finally let \(\tau_t\) be the target after replacing the contrast by \((3+t,-1-t,-1,-1)\).  For every schedule,
\[
 |\tau_t(Y)-\tau_0(Y)|
 =\left|{t\over6}\sum_{g,i}\{Y_{gi}(1,1)-Y_{gi}(0,1)\}\right|
 \le |t|.                                                                  \tag{49}
\]
For either design class, Minkowski's inequality applied before the supremum over \(Y\), followed by infimization over procedures, gives
\[
 \left|\sqrt{R_t}-\sqrt{R_0}\right|\le|t|.                                \tag{50}
\]
One may take a common unrestricted estimator space in (50), since projection onto the target interval cannot increase squared error.  The constant-zero rule and \(|\tau_0|\le3\) give \(\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{ind},0}},\sqrt{R^star_0}\le3\).  Therefore (48)--(50) imply
\[
 R_{\mathrm{ind},t}-R^star_t
 >0.000918578-2|t|
   \{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{ind},0}}+\sqrt{R^star_0}\}
 \ge0.000918578-12|t|>0.0007                                               \tag{51}
\]
whenever \(|t|\le10^{-5}\).  Rational \(t\) preserves the rational contrast and its zero coefficient sum, completing the claimed infinite rational neighborhood.
